summary: Every Arabic noun is masculine or feminine. Most feminine nouns end in tāʾ marbūṭa ـة (غُرْفَة، شَقَّة، طَاوِلَة); nouns for women are feminine whatever their ending (بِنْت، أُمّ); and some nouns are feminine with no ة at all — كَأْس (glass), دَار (house), شَمْس (sun), أَرْض (earth), and body parts that come in pairs (يَد، عَيْن، رِجْل). Everything else is masculine. Gender decides “this” (هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ), “it” (هُوَ / هِيَ), and later adjectives and verbs. Nouns for people come in pairs: طَالِب / طَالِبَة, مُعَلِّم / مُعَلِّمَة.

blocks.title: People: a masculine and a feminine.
blocks.text: طَالِب → طَالِبَة, مُعَلِّم → مُعَلِّمَة, صَدِيق → صَدِيقَة: add ة. Plurals: طُلَّاب / طَالِبَات, مُعَلِّمُونَ / مُعَلِّمَات, أَصْدِقَاء / صَدِيقَات. A mixed group takes the masculine plural.

blocks.title: Masculine with ة.
blocks.text: A few masculine nouns end in ة: خَلِيفَة (caliph), and men’s names such as حَمْزَة and أُسَامَة. The meaning (a man) wins.

blocks.title: Test with “this” and “it”.
blocks.text: Not sure? Use the noun with هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ or answer with هُوَ / هِيَ: هٰذِهِ كَأْسٌ — الْكَأْسُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا.
A collective noun (وَرَق paper, بَصَل onions) is masculine; its unit noun in ة is feminine: وَرَق → وَرَقَة (a sheet of paper).
مَاء (water) ends in -āʾ but is masculine: its hamza belongs to the root, it is not the feminine ending.

askYourself: Does it end in ـة? → feminine (unless it names a man: خَلِيفَة).
Does it name a woman or a girl? → feminine.
Is it one of the feminines without ة (كَأْس، دَار، شَمْس، أَرْض، نَار) or a paired body part? → feminine.
Does it end in the feminine -āʾ / -ā (صَحْرَاء، كُبْرَى)? → feminine — but مَاء is masculine.

traps: كَأْس is feminine: هٰذِهِ كَأْسٌ, not *هٰذَا كَأْسٌ.
بِنْت ends in ت, not ة — and is feminine.
Plurals of things agree as feminine singular whatever the gender of the singular: كِتَاب (m.) → هٰذِهِ الْكُتُبُ.
Gender belongs to the word, not to the thing: بَيْت is masculine and شَمْس feminine — even where another language gives them another gender.

quiz.why: One of the feminines without ة: هٰذِهِ كَأْسٌ.
No ة, not a woman, not on the list of exceptions → masculine.
The others are feminine: two end in ة, and بِنْت is a girl.
كَأْس is feminine; no article → a sentence.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew has the same two genders and the same main sign (feminine -ָה / -ֶת), with feminines that lack it (אֶרֶץ, earth) — and כּוֹס (glass) is feminine there too.
German has three genders that the form rarely shows — learn der / die / das with every noun; Arabic gender is mostly visible (ة).
Chinese nouns have no gender; he / she / it differ only in the writing (他 / 她 / 它).

notes.text: Greek has three genders and the ending often shows them (-ος, -η / -α, -ο); Arabic has two, with ة as the main feminine sign. The genders often differ: ο ήλιος is masculine but شَمْس feminine; το σπίτι is neuter, بَيْت masculine.
Russian has three genders, shown by the ending; Arabic has two, with ة as the main feminine sign — and no neuter: a Russian neuter such as окно becomes feminine نَافِذَة.
Spanish also has two genders with a typical feminine ending (-a ≈ ة: mesa ≈ طَاوِلَة). There are exceptions on both sides: la mano is feminine like يَد, el día masculine.
English nouns have no grammatical gender; every Arabic noun is masculine or feminine, and “this”, “it”, adjectives and verbs follow it.
French also has two genders, but the noun rarely shows it; Arabic gender is mostly visible: ة means feminine (غُرْفَة), with a short list of exceptions.
Hindi also has two genders and a typical feminine ending (-ī: लड़की); the Arabic sign is ة. Loanwords can switch gender: किताब is feminine in Hindi, كِتَاب masculine in Arabic.
Persian nouns have no gender; in Arabic every noun is masculine or feminine — learn it with the word (ة is the main sign).
Marathi has three genders, Arabic two, so Marathi neuters become masculine or feminine (घर is neuter, بَيْت masculine).
Turkish has no gender; in Arabic you must know whether each noun is masculine or feminine — ة is the main sign.
Japanese nouns have no gender; Arabic nouns are masculine or feminine, and the words that point to them agree.
Finnish nouns have no gender (hän is he and she); Arabic nouns are masculine or feminine, and the pronoun shows it: الْغُرْفَةُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا.
Hungarian nouns have no gender; in Arabic each noun is masculine or feminine.
Swahili sorts nouns into classes by prefix (m- / wa-, ki- / vi- …); Arabic has two classes only, masculine and feminine, marked mostly by an ending (ة), not a prefix.
Luganda noun classes are marked by prefixes (omu-, eki- …); Arabic’s two genders are marked mostly by the ending ة and are tied to sex for people.
Vietnamese nouns have no gender — classifiers group them instead; Arabic nouns are masculine or feminine, and everything that refers to them agrees.
Inuktitut nouns have no gender; Arabic splits every noun into masculine and feminine.
